Save this file as `ch4-practice/analysis/ex-4-1.qmd` and fill it in during class. The answers are on the course website, under Exercises, Ex-4-1. Try each task before you look.

**Every task has four steps, in this order.** They are the way of working with AI from lecture 03-1, "Working with AI on your own research"; today you use it for figures.

1. **Look** at the data, or at the figure, before anyone writes code.
2. **Predict.** Write down the message the figure must convey, who reads it, and what a figure that conveys it would show.
3. **Ask.** Start from the recommended request in the task. Replace every `<...>` with what only you know. Send it to your AI assistant.
4. **Render and read.** The AI's code goes into this file under the task's heading. Render this file to HTML, open the HTML, and judge the figure there, at the size a reader will see it.

A chat assistant cannot edit or render this file: paste its chunks into the task's code chunk and render yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.

**Rules:**

A. Write the message and the reader **before** you ask the AI.

B. Keep the request you actually sent in this file, with the blanks filled in.

C. When the AI offers several designs, choose one and write why, in terms of the message.

D. You judge a figure by reading the rendered HTML, not the chat window.

# The figure standard

Every figure request in this worksheet ends with this block, pasted just before the closing instructions. Copy it from here each time. Keep your own copy for later work, and add to it whenever you find something the AI keeps getting wrong.

```text
Every figure must meet this standard:
1. Axis titles, legend titles and category labels in plain words with
   units, such as "Corn yield (bushels per acre)", never a column name;
   categories in words, such as "Irrigated", never a code such as 1.
2. Tick labels, axis titles and legend text no smaller than the
   document's body text, at the size the figure appears in the HTML.
3. No legend when lines or points can be labelled directly or there is
   only one group. Otherwise, the legend inside an empty corner of the
   plot, or above or below a wide figure, in the same order as the lines
   or bars it describes.
4. Numbers formatted for reading: thousands separators, no more decimals
   than the message needs, percentages shown as percentages.
5. No overlapping tick labels; for long category names, put the
   categories on the vertical axis rather than rotating the text.
6. Light or no gridlines and no heavy borders, so the data is the
   darkest thing in the figure.
7. A shape that suits the content: wide for a change over time, close
   to square for a relationship between two variables.
8. Colours readable by colour-blind readers (such as the Okabe-Ito
   palette), and no more colours than the message needs.
```

# Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure

The message this figure is meant to convey: **"Long extreme droughts cut corn yields in all three states, by roughly 20 bushels per acre."**

```{r}
#| label: task-5-weak
#| message: false
library(ggplot2)
county_yield <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "county_yield.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

ggplot(county_yield, aes(drought_weeks, corn_yield, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_point()
```
